thread.title: Purdue leads initiative for semiconductor talent shortage - NewsBreak

author: STAFF REPORTS
title: Purdue leads initiative for semiconductor talent shortage - NewsBreak
text:
By STAFF REPORTS ,
7 hours ago Photo provided by Purdue University Purdue University’s Chipshub, hosted on Purdue’s existing nanoHUB system, is leading the initiative to boost the availability of workforce talent in the semiconductor industry by providing free online access to cutting-edge simulation tools used to design chips.
To build the platform, Purdue partnered with industry leaders, including Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens, as well as federal agencies including the U.S. Department of War and the U.S. National Science Foundation.
“This initiative reduces the cost and time for adoption of electronic design automation tools in the classroom and empowers universities across the United States – particularly non-research-intensive institutions — to train the next generation of semiconductor engineers and technicians,” according to Alejandro Strachan, Purdue’s Reilly Professor of Materials Engineering and co-director of nanoHUB/Chipshub, on the Purdue News website.
Globally, the U.S. semiconductor sector designs 52% of chips and is experiencing a dire supply need due to AI, 5G, and advanced manufacturing. By 2030, the workforce is projected to need 115,000 more jobs. However, current projections indicate that 50% of these jobs have a risk of being unoccupied, according to the 2023 report issued by the Semiconductor Industry Association.
Traditional barriers to access electronic design automation tools, such as costs, installation requirements, and maintenance, have affected non-research-intensive universities, which educate a significant portion of students but lack the resources of research-focused institutions. This initiative allows universities to integrate EDA tools into the classroom.
Kerrie Douglas, co-director of Purdue University’s Scalable Asymmetric Lifecycle Engagement program, said the nanoHUB partnership goes beyond a learning concept by offering SCALE students hands-on experience with industry tools, according to the Purdue News website.
By widening access to over 100 U.S. universities, the initiative hopes to reach tens of thousands of students and be able to foster a broader, inclusive future workforce, and boost the U.S. competitiveness in global supply chains.
